practices.title: Self-directed keyboard consolidation
practices.description: Rework any needed drills ad lib. Reach out and play one, two, or three tones and chords. If certain tones are confused, work those tones. practices.title: Self-directed guitar reference weaning
practices.description: Extend the previous string work to B and E strings. Use two- and three-note chords. Go among A, D, G, B, E strings, adding more any tones between references and returning less often. Choose the drills according to your own judgment. On your guitar extend A/D/G work to B and E strings and two-/three-note chords. Gradually put more tones between references as needed. You choose when to return: there is no fixed reference cadence or automatically scheduled weaning sequence.

info.purpose: Check how guitarists extend string work and gradually reduce dependence on reference tones.
info.source_audio: David Lucas Burge - Master Class 23 - The Perfect Pitch Ear Training SuperCourse [-UBt5aS1k2Q].mp3

source_windows.description: Extend to B/E strings and two-/three-note chords; add more tones between reference returns.
No fixed drill is assigned: use judgment, return to references less often, and work until the tones feel established.

info.skill: identify tones with decreasing reference dependence
source_instructions: Extend the previous string work to B and E strings.
Use two- and three-note chords.
Go among A, D, G, B, E strings, adding more any tones between references and returning less often.
Choose the drills according to your own judgment.
info.presentation: Self-directed adaptation of existing string drills.

completion.details: Work until you feel you have got the tones; no fixed drill is assigned.

evidence.quote: Same with solo guitarists. You can see what to do. You see what we've done with our A string, our D string, and our G string.
Now you can work your other strings. Work your B string the same way. Work your E strings the same way.
Do two- and three-note chords. Do the same thing. Go back and forth between A string,
D string, G string, B string, and E string, and have the repetitions become less. Color
awareness is becoming grounded. Your ear has been thoroughly prepared. You'll figure out how to work
your strings in any way you need to gradually wean yourself from needing your reference tone.
Every time we go back to our A string or our D string or our G string, then we're needing a reference tone.
But add more tones in between your reference tones as you go.
I'm not giving you any drill this time. This is all up to you now.
It's your professional judgment at this point.
Come back to your tones less and less.
Add more any tones as you're going, because it's the any tones that are testing you for perfect pitch.
You have to be skillful here, but I'm very confident that you can complete this drill.
Work with your tones and your strings any way that you feel you need to until you feel you've got the tones.
This is your final step to color discrimination.

prerequisites: Previous A-, D-, and G-string work.
uncertainties: No specified interval between references or numerical criterion.

practices.title: Team random rounds and targeted backtracking
practices.description: Test one another in random rounds with all tones. Drill weaknesses, including difficult three-tone chords. Return to three diminished-seventh patterns or scales if helpful. Optionally redo comfortable lessons in a new key, for example E major. With a partner, identify random full-set tones and chords, remediate weaknesses and optionally revisit separate diminished patterns or scales in another key. Readiness is self-assessed; 100% accuracy is explicitly NOT required.

info.purpose: Check partner-led remediation, backtracking options, and qualitative readiness rather than a new fixed quota.

patterns if you need to you can go back to scales if you want just test each other finally play
tones identify the tones if you find weaknesses with particular tones drill those areas if you
you find that three-tone chords are difficult in any way, maybe with the black, maybe with the
white tones, whatever. Work those areas. Smooth them out. And you can take a break and go to scales.

E major scale all over again. There's many different things that you can do. You can
backtrack to any comfortable lesson and rework the whole thing in a new key if you want.
